transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2026-03-04 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Samira Gomez (Redwood SE), Nate Brooks (Redwood SE - optional), Dr. Priya Kapoor (HelixAI Head of ML), Liam O'Neil (HelixAI Infra), Marcus Lee (HelixAI CTO), Sofia Ramos (HelixAI Security)

Summary: Deep dive on runtime perf trade-offs across Llama/Mistral/Qwen families; RoPE scaling, MoE routing cost/throughput, KV cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run a benchmark in customer VPC and share quantization config.

Topics: runtime latency/throughput, KV cache hit patterns, batching windows, int8/awq quantization impacts, MoE routing overhead, rope scaling and sequence length tradeoffs, private deployment network egress and KMS integration.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll run through architecture-specific tuning for Llama, Mistral and Qwen plus MoE bits and RoPE scaling. Samira's gonna lead on perf.
[00:24] Samira Gomez: hi, yeah, quick agenda, um, first runway numbers, then KV cache behaviour, batching and then quantization and deploy notes - VPC / on-prem specifics at the end. Sound ok?
[00:35] Priya Kapoor: yes thanks, our main goals are: keep p95 latency below 200ms for text-gen flows, and cost per 1k tokens under our target. We also care about private keys in our VPC and audit logs.
[00:50] Samira Gomez: ok, good. Quick background, we evaluated Llama 2 and Mistral on-host; Qwen is newer for you, right?
[00:57] Marcus Lee: correct, we're prototyping Qwen for higher context windows. We also have an MoE proposal for the summarization pipeline.
[01:12] Liam O'Neil: and infra constraints: our VPC runs across two AZs, limited egress to public internet, and on-prem lab with 4x A100s for heavy tests.
[01:26] Samira Gomez: got it. So first, RoPE scaling — as sequence length increases, RoPE rotary embeddings change the attention frequency interactions; practically we see increasing memory and slightly higher per-token latency. For Llama-style models, long RoPE scaling can increase KV cache pressure.
[01:48] Priya Kapoor: we saw token runtime jump at 4k context and again at 16k on Mistral — is that expected?
[01:55] Samira Gomez: yes, partially. Mistral tends to have denser attention compute per token at longer seqs; also kernel selection matters — some CUDA kernels are optimized for 2k/4k boundaries. If you jump to 16k, you cross to different kernel paths, causing latency jumps.
[02:15] Jordan Patel: one trick is to tune the compile-time tiling and limit the effective context window when you don't need the full 16k for every request, and use dynamic prefix caching.
[02:27] Marcus Lee: about KV cache: we currently store per-request KV in Redis, but we see high mem churn when many concurrent sessions hit long contexts. Any suggestions?
[02:39] Samira Gomez: yeah storing raw KV in Redis works but is expensive for large keys; we often recommend Redwood's prefix/KV cache layer with sharded eviction and LRU heuristics — reduces egress and memory. But with private deployments you can also mount local NVMe cache to store serialized KV to avoid network roundtrips.
[03:01] Liam O'Neil: how conservative is the cache invalidation? We need strict privacy controls.
[03:07] Samira Gomez: can configure TTLs and per-customer key encryption; in VPC/on-prem you control KMS. We support envelope encryption and key rotation; Sofia we can share our KMS integration notes.
[03:18] Sofia Ramos: yes please, need the exact flow for HSM + audit logs.
[03:23] Jordan Patel: noted, we'll send SOC2 docs and KMS flow.
[03:26] Samira Gomez: moving on — batching: continuous batching at the runtime layer helps throughput but can increase p95 if batching windows are too long. We typically recommend dynamic batching with a max latency budget of 20-50ms for low-latency apps; for higher throughput off-hours you can increase the window.
[03:47] Priya Kapoor: our p95 target is 200ms so what's safe?
[03:50] Samira Gomez: with dynamic batching and GPU pooling, you can keep p95 sub-200ms for medium tokens (<=512) on Mistral 8B with proper KV caching; but for Qwen with 32k contexts, you might need dedicated nodes to keep p95 steady because memory swaps can spike.
[04:10] Marcus Lee: dedicated nodes meaning Redwood Dedicated or our reserved on-prem nodes?
[04:14] Samira Gomez: both options, Redwood Dedicated gives predictable throughput; for on-prem you'd pin GPUs and tune kernel comps — our runtime can run in both.
[04:22] Jordan Patel: let's talk MoE — Priya mentioned summarization. MoE models route tokens to experts which saves FLOPs for some workloads, but routing has overhead. Samira?
[04:34] Samira Gomez: routing cost is mostly extra gather/scatter ops and memory movement. At small batch sizes routing overhead proportionally hurts latency. For high throughput (batched requests) MoE can be more efficient, but you must account for imbalance — routing imbalance causes some experts to be hot and saturate memory/bandwidth.
[04:56] Liam O'Neil: is there an easy way to model cost per token for MoE?
[04:59] Samira Gomez: we typically produce a cost model: base transformer cost + routing overhead (x%) + expert compute cost. We'll share a spreadsheet. For HelixAI's workload, if summarization is long-form and high QPS, MoE probably saves cost; for low QPS with tight p95, a dense model might be better.
[05:21] Priya Kapoor: earlier you mentioned routing to fallback dense experts to reduce imbalance — can you expand?
[05:26] Samira Gomez: yes, things like load-balancing loss during training, or at runtime using jittered routing decisions, or blending with a dense backbone. In Redwood we have fallbacks to compatible dense variants to avoid 503s during expert overload.
[05:40] Marcus Lee: about quantization — we've tried awq 4-bit on Llama and saw weird tokenization artifacts. Any gotchas with Qwen/Mistral?
[05:51] Samira Gomez: awq/int8 can be model-sensitive. Qwen weights and normalization layers require careful calibration; Mistral's group norms can be more robust. Also watch for activation quantization — per-channel quant vs per-tensor changes things. We suggest running eval prompts and automated regen tests.
[06:11] Jordan Patel: we'll send our eval set. Samira: what's implication for latency with int8/awq?
[06:16] Samira Gomez: int8 lowers memory bandwidth and can increase throughput by 1.5-3x depending on kernel support; latency improves but calibration time and one-off artifacts need evaluation. On some GPUs int8 matmuls are faster, but on older ones you might not see the same gains.
[06:33] Liam O'Neil: our on-prem A100s support int8 but we haven't run AWQ optim. Samira: do you recommend compile step?
[06:41] Samira Gomez: yes — compile with quantized kernels and fusing ops. Our compilation picks kernel variants based on seq len, batch and quant mode. We'll give a sample compile profile.
[06:53] Jordan Patel: NETWORK concerns — VPC peering and private deployments: what about cold-starts and image pulls for on-prem lab?
[07:01] Samira Gomez: for on-prem, pre-warm the runtime on GPUs, and pre-pull model shards to local storage; for VPCs restrict outbound to only Redwood artifact registry or use an internal mirror. Pull speed affects cold-start. We can provide container images for air-gapped installs.
[07:19] Priya Kapoor: about audit logs and multi-tenant separation, can we get token-level tracing?
[07:25] Jordan Patel: yes, Redwood console offers token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards and trace hooks you can ship to your logging stack in VPC.
[07:34] Sofia Ramos: and for keys: HSM or customer KMS?
[07:38] Jordan Patel: both supported. For private we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; we store only envelope encrypted artifacts. We'll share the key flow doc.
[07:48] Marcus Lee: any limitations with Qwen and rope scaling for very long contexts like 64k?
[07:54] Samira Gomez: 64k brings new problems: KV cache size grows linearly, attention compute goes up quadratically if you do dense attention; for Qwen there are sparse attention kernels but the compiler choice and memory placement matter. We often recommend a hybrid approach: sparse attention + sliding window + local KV retention.
[08:14] Priya Kapoor: sliding window plus recency cache could work for our agents.
[08:19] Samira Gomez: exactly — keep the high-signal recent tokens in fast NVMe-backed cache, and summarize older context into compressed memory vectors.
[08:28] Liam O'Neil: any GPU recommendations? We have A100s and limited 80GB V100s.
[08:33] Samira Gomez: A100-80GB good for big Qwen variants; for Mistral and Llama 8–13B you can use 40GB A100 with sharding. For MoE experts, you may want more memory per GPU or expert placement across devices.
[08:50] Jordan Patel: let's touch on telemetry and regressions: how do you prevent quantization/regression surprises?
[08:56] Samira Gomez: Redwood Optimize includes eval hooks: run prompt suites when you change quantization or kernels and produce quality regressions alerts. Integrate your eval set in CI. We'll share the eval template.
[09:08] Priya Kapoor: awesome. Ok, more practical: for our benchmark can we start with Mistral 7B and Qwen-16k with awq-4bit and compare?
[09:18] Samira Gomez: yes, start with those two; we'll provide the compile bundles and batch configs. For MoE we should test dense vs MoE on a subset of traffic.
[09:28] Marcus Lee: what about fallback routing when an expert is overloaded? Does Redwood do automatic fallback?
[09:34] Samira Gomez: yes we have automatic fallback to compatible dense variants or alternate experts; you can set policies like retry, queue, or degrade to a smaller model. That keeps the app from failing.
[09:44] Liam O'Neil: pricing impact of MoE?
[09:47] Jordan Patel: MoE can lower compute cost per token at scale but may need more memory footprint and network traffic; we'll share a cost model that outlines routing overhead, expert hot-spots and estimate tokens/sec for Helix's profile.
[10:00] Samira Gomez: note: routing hot-spot mitigation includes expert capacity doubling, jittered routing, and in-train smoothing; all affect effective cost and latency.
[10:09] Priya Kapoor: ok good. A few quick clarifications: 1) KV cache retention policy defaults? 2) recommended batch target for 99th percentile? 3) how we integrate KMS?
[10:20] Samira Gomez: 1) default TTL is 30m but customizable per-route; 2) aim for batching window 20–30ms for p99 budgets under 200ms but you'll profile; 3) we support envelope encryption with customer KMS — we'll send doc.
[10:36] Jordan Patel: we're out of time but let's recap next steps.
[10:40] Priya Kapoor: recap: run benchmark in VPC, share quant config, SOC2 + KMS flow, MoE cost spreadsheet.
[10:47] Jordan Patel: yes, Samira will send compile/quant bundles and benchmark template; I'll attach SOC2 and key docs.
[10:53] Samira Gomez: I'll also include recommended batching and caching configs and an example of on-prem pre-warm steps.
[10:58] Marcus Lee: thanks, we'll get the VPC details and expected QPS by Monday.
[11:03] Jordan Patel: perfect, thanks everyone. End.
